title: Lexecon Inc. v. Milberg Weiss Bershad Hynes & Lerach (1998)
summary: The MDL transferee court could not assign a transferred action to itself for trial in disregard of § 1407’s remand requirement.
notes:
The detailed underlying litigation facts are not reproduced there. The note’s later discussion of possible waiver is not a holding that parties can never consent to trial in the transferee forum.

Lexecon sued the Milberg Weiss and Cotchett firms in Illinois for malicious prosecution; the Judicial Panel transferred the case to Arizona for pretrial proceedings, and the Arizona court then transferred it to itself for trial under 1404(a). Justice Souter wrote for a unanimous Court (Justice Scalia did not join Part II-C).

sections.Parties: Lexecon and the opposing parties litigated an action that had been transferred for multidistrict pretrial proceedings.
sections.Material Facts: The transferee court sought to retain the transferred action for trial by using § 1404(a). That approach followed a longstanding practice that the Judicial Panel’s rules had accommodated. The relevant statutory language, however, required remand to the original court when the authorized pretrial proceedings ended.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court rejected the self-assignment practice and enforced the remand duty.
sections.Issue: Could the transferee court use § 1404(a) to keep the MDL-transferred case for trial?
sections.Holding: No. Section 1407 imposed a remand duty that the proposed self-assignment could not evade.
sections.Reasoning: The statutory purpose of pretrial coordination did not authorize a different trial forum through longstanding administrative practice alone. The Court enforced the enacted limit while reserving a separate question about § 1404(a)’s wording permitting transfer to another district. The note then discusses later waiver questions and choice-of-law implications, which require separate analysis.

learning.why: The MDL transferee court could not assign a transferred action to itself for trial in disregard of § 1407’s remand requirement.

topics.cp-mdl: Section 1407’s remand duty limited the transferee court’s power to retain a transferred case for trial.
topics.cp-transfer: The court could not evade that duty by assigning the transferred action to itself under § 1404.
topics.cp-statute-interpretation: The Court rejected a longstanding self-assignment practice inconsistent with the statutory requirement.
topics.cp-usc-1407: The holding construes the mandatory 'shall be remanded' language of 1407(a).
topics.cp-usc-1404: The Court rejected using 1404(a) as a vehicle for a transferee court to assign an MDL case to itself for trial.

mnemonic.rationale: A case transferred back to itself
